SMSA's consist of an entire county or counties, so they have the added attraction of being drawn along readily identifiable political boundaries. Nevertheless, we concluded in the Interim Report that certain countervailing factors militate against use of the SMSA concept to determine the geographic scope of section 203(b)(8). The designation of SMSA's on a county-wide basis means that if any part of an adjacent county meets the economic and social criteria for integration with the central city, the entire county is This often results in the inclusion included in the SMSA. of a considerable amount of territory which is not ordinarily considered "urban" and does not meet the general requirements for being considered "commercially a part of" and "adjacent to" the base municipality in terms of local urban transportation. There is also a large regional disparity in SMSA size, which does not correspond to relative degrees of urban development. County lines have been drawn in many western States to include large territorial tracts; therefore, SMSA's in the West tend to be much larger than those in the East. Furthermore, use of the SMSA concept would require a tripartite approach - SMSA, SCSA, and an expanded population-mileage formula. We believe it preferable to
In certain areas where there is a continuously developed, high density population having certain metropolitan commuting patterns, two or more SMSA's have been combined into a Standard Consolidated Statistical Area (SCSA). The SCSA criteria are set out in Appendix B to the Interim Report, Commercial Zones, 124 M.C.C. at 198.
In many regions of the country no SMSAs or SCSAs have been designated, either because insufficient concentrated population exists or because proper data have not yet been collected.
